questions.question: How are sorted document IDs converted to gaps?
options: Keep the first ID, then store each successive difference
Subtract every document ID from the final document ID
Store the difference between each ID and the vocabulary size
Replace each ID with the count of its stored positions

questions.question: How are gap-encoded document IDs decoded?
options: By sorting the gaps into descending order
By multiplying every gap by the term frequency
By computing the cumulative prefix sums
By hashing each gap into a document bucket

questions.question: Why do frequent terms often require fewer bits per posting?
options: Their document IDs are stored without any ordering
Their postings are stored uncompressed for fast decode
Their absolute document IDs are smaller than a rare term's
Dense occurrence across documents produces small gaps

questions.question: Why do compressed blocks store an absolute base or last document ID?
options: It gives a restart point for skipping into the delta stream
It makes every gap inside the block equal to zero
It removes the need to keep document IDs in sorted order
It converts token positions into source character offsets

questions.question: Why can random external document IDs hurt gap compression?
options: They guarantee that every term posting is locally dense
They destroy the locality that produces small gaps
They prevent the postings list from being sorted at all
They force every gap into a fixed seven-bit width

questions.question: How many payload bits does each variable-byte byte carry?
options: Four
Six
Seven
Eight

questions.question: Under a seven-bit payload scheme, which values fit in one byte?
options: 0 through 63
0 through 255
128 through 16,383
0 through 127

questions.question: Why does integer 130 require two variable-byte payload groups?
options: It equals 1 times 128 plus a remainder of 2
Every integer above 64 needs at least four bytes
Its decimal digits are split across two groups
The first group stores the term's document frequency

questions.question: What is a main advantage of variable-byte over one fixed block width?
options: It stores every integer in exactly one byte-aligned slot
A large outlier uses more bytes without widening its neighbors
It gives constant-time random access to any encoded integer
It drops the marker bit and uses all eight bits as payload

questions.question: Why is random access into a raw variable-byte gap stream difficult?
options: Every byte independently stores one absolute document ID
The stream carries no terminal markers to align against
A byte offset can land mid-integer, and prior gaps set the IDs
Variable-byte values are always stored in descending order

questions.question: How should a decoder handle a malformed sequence with no terminal byte?
options: Continue reading indefinitely until the storage ends
Treat the incomplete value as document ID zero
Reverse the continuation convention and retry the read
Fail within a bounded length to prevent runaway reads

questions.question: What principle do postings and Parquet encodings share?
options: Transform values into low-entropy residuals before coding
Store every value as an uncompressed fixed-width string field
Avoid sorting, because ordering makes differences larger
Use one general codec regardless of the access pattern

questions.question: Which Parquet encoding most directly resembles postings gap encoding?
options: Plain string encoding
Delta binary packing
Dictionary index encoding
Nested repetition levels

questions.question: Why do postings codecs emphasize restart points and skips?
options: Search decompresses the complete index for every query
Postings lists never require any selective traversal
Interactive scoring must jump without decoding earlier values
Parquet row groups carry no metadata that enables pruning

questions.question: How does Parquet typically consume encoded data?
options: One value at a time with no column selection at all
A complete object decompressed for every single row key
One postings list traversed for each query term
Selected column pages decoded into vectorized batches

questions.question: Why might a hot postings list reject a slightly smaller whole-stream Zstd representation?
options: It can harm selective skipping and add decode latency
General-purpose compression expands every integer stream
Postings lists are never read during an interactive query
Whole-stream compression gives constant-time access to a posting

questions.question: What is the right evaluation metric for either compression system?
options: Maximum ratio, measured without any query or scan
Work avoided per unit of CPU under the real read pattern
The number of codec names the file format supports
Compressed size measured only on uniform random integers
